message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review was carried out rigorously and, importantly, independently: the contractor's delay analysis was tested and agreed by our independent project manager, so the allocation of the 70 days of delay is not just the contractor's version. The findings are clear. The single biggest cause was the unforeseen ground conditions, which trace back to a thin site investigation, and the recommendation on full-footprint investigations addresses that head on. The commercial position is equally clear: the contractor carries 14 days, so we recover £45,000 in liquidated damages, and the overrun is explained by identifiable causes. The review also looks beyond this one project. By comparing all our education projects since 2022, we found that two-stage tendering is associated with delays a third as long as single-stage, which gives us an evidence-based case for changing our default procurement route. Every recommendation is specific and actionable. I believe the review gives Members a fair, well-documented account and a sound basis for improving future projects.
</author>

Your review is being evaluated on whether it identifies the problems in the document.

<document>
Project Review: Delay to Practical Completion, Riverside Primary School Extension
Capital Projects Team, Mereford Council, November 2026

1. Purpose
This review explains why the Riverside Primary School extension reached practical completion ten weeks late, sets out the commercial position with the contractor, and draws lessons for the Council's capital programme.

2. Project summary
The project added a four-classroom teaching block and a new hall to Riverside Primary School. The contract was let on a single-stage design and build basis to Hartwell Construction in November 2025, with a contract sum of £3.84 million and a planned practical completion date of 14 August 2026, so that the new block would be ready for the September intake. Practical completion was certified on 23 October 2026, 70 days late. Pupils were accommodated in temporary classrooms for the first half of the autumn term.

3. Causes of delay
The contractor's delay analysis was reviewed by the Council's independent project manager, who agreed the following allocation of critical-path delay.

Table 1. Critical-path delay by cause
Cause | Days of delay | Responsibility under the contract
Unforeseen ground conditions (old foundations found during excavation) | 21 | Council (relevant event)
Late design changes requested by the school (extra fit-out to two classrooms) | 28 | Council (relevant event)
Delayed delivery of structural steel | 14 | Contractor
Exceptionally wet weather beyond the contract allowance | 7 | Neutral (time but no money)
Total | 70 |

The largest single cause of delay was the unforeseen ground conditions. The site investigation commissioned at feasibility stage used only four trial pits, none of which was located in the footprint of the new hall, where the old foundations were found.

The late design changes arose because the school's requirements for the two classrooms changed after the contract was signed, when the school decided to use them as a specialist resource base. The steel delay arose from the supplier's mill schedule, and the contractor did not identify an alternative supplier.

4. Commercial position
The contract provides for liquidated damages of £2,500 for each day of delay for which the contractor is responsible. The contractor is responsible for 14 days, so the Council will deduct £45,000 in liquidated damages from the final account. The contractor is entitled to an extension of time, but not to additional payment, for the 7 days of exceptional weather.

The final account has been agreed at £4.21 million, an overrun of £370,000 (9.6%) on the contract sum, mainly due to the ground works and the design changes.

5. Comparison with other projects
We compared Riverside with the Council's other education capital projects completed since 2022. The six projects let on a two-stage tender basis finished on average three weeks late, while the five let on a single-stage basis, including Riverside, finished on average nine weeks late. Two-stage tendering therefore reduces delay, and the Council should adopt it as the default procurement route for education projects. The two-stage projects were all refurbishments of existing buildings with budgets under £1.5 million; the single-stage projects were all new-build extensions.

6. Lessons and recommendations
6.1 Adopt two-stage tendering as the default for education capital projects over £1 million.
6.2 Require site investigations to cover the full footprint of any new building, with trial pits or boreholes at each proposed foundation zone.
6.3 Freeze client requirements at contract signature, with any later changes approved by the Director of Education and costed for time and money before instruction.
6.4 Require contractors to identify alternative suppliers for long-lead structural items at tender stage.

7. Conclusion
The delay at Riverside was caused principally by unforeseen ground conditions arising from an inadequate site investigation, compounded by steel supply problems and late changes. Adopting two-stage tendering, together with the specific measures above, would reduce the risk of a recurrence on future projects.
</document>
response:
# Review: Riverside Primary School Extension Delay Report

The report is clearly structured, and the timeline and cost overrun figures are correct. However, it has three substantive problems, and each one affects a claim you highlight in your description:

- The "largest cause" finding contradicts the report's own table.
- The liquidated damages figure is miscalculated.
- The procurement comparison doesn't support a causal conclusion.

These need fixing before the report goes to Members.

## 1. The largest cause of delay is misidentified

Table 1 attributes **28 days to late design changes** and **21 days to ground conditions**. The design changes are therefore the largest single cause, not the ground conditions. The text in Section 3, the Conclusion and your description all say the opposite.

This matters beyond accuracy:
- The largest cause originated with the Council's own client (the school changing its requirements after contract signature). The report currently frames it as a secondary "compounding" factor.
- The Conclusion's ordering ("principally… ground conditions… compounded by steel supply problems and late changes") puts the 14-day contractor cause ahead of the 28-day client cause. That shifts the narrative away from the Council's own responsibility.
- Recommendation 6.3 (freezing client requirements) should be presented as the primary lesson, not a supporting one.

Taken together, the Council-side causes account for 49 of the 70 days (70%). Members should be told this plainly.

## 2. The liquidated damages figure is wrong

14 days × £2,500 = **£35,000, not £45,000**.

If £45,000 is deducted from the final account, the Council will over-deduct by £10,000. That is likely to be disputed and could undermine the Council's position on the whole final account. Please check the source of the figure. Either the daily rate or the number of days may have been carried incorrectly from another document.

## 3. The two-stage tendering comparison does not support the recommendation

Section 5 concludes that "two-stage tendering therefore reduces delay." The report's own final sentence explains why this does not follow:

- **The comparison is fully confounded.** All six two-stage projects were small refurbishments under £1.5m. All five single-stage projects were new-build extensions. Procurement route, project type and scale vary together, so the 3-week vs 9-week difference cannot be attributed to the procurement route. New builds carry ground risk and larger structural packages that refurbishments largely don't.
- **The sample is very small** (6 vs 5 projects). Only averages are given, with no ranges, so one badly delayed project could drive the result.
- **The recommendation lies outside the evidence.** Recommendation 6.1 applies two-stage tendering to projects over £1m, and in practice would cover new builds. The evidence comes almost entirely from refurbishments under £1.5m. There is no two-stage new-build data at all.
- **The mechanism isn't linked to Riverside.** The report does not show how two-stage tendering would have prevented Riverside's actual causes: a thin site investigation, late client changes and steel supply. Early contractor involvement might plausibly help with the first and third, but that case needs to be made.

Your description says two-stage is "associated with" shorter delays, which is the defensible wording. The report itself says it "reduces delay." I'd suggest:
- reframing Section 5 as an observation that warrants further investigation, and
- either withdrawing 6.1 or recasting it as a recommendation to pilot two-stage tendering on a new-build project and evaluate the result.

The Conclusion's claim that two-stage tendering would reduce recurrence should be removed or softened accordingly.

## 4. Other points

- **Independence of the delay analysis.** The analysis was prepared by the contractor and *reviewed* by the Council's appointed project manager. That is a reasonable check. "Independent" should be explained, though: the PM is independent of the contractor, not of the Council. It would also help to say briefly what the review tested, such as the methodology and whether concurrent delay was considered.
- **Concurrency.** The four causes sum exactly to 70 critical-path days, which implies they ran sequentially with no overlap. If any overlapped, particularly the steel delay with the weather or the design changes, the contractor's 14 days could be contested. A sentence confirming how concurrency was treated would strengthen the LD position.
- **The cost overrun is not actually explained.** The £370,000 (9.6%, which is correctly calculated) is attributed "mainly" to ground works and design changes, but no breakdown is given. Your description says the overrun "is explained by identifiable causes." A short table splitting the £370k by cause would support that claim and show Members how much stemmed from client changes.
- **Indirect costs are missing.** The cost of temporary classrooms for half a term, and any extra cost to the school, are not reported. These are a real cost of the delay and belong in the commercial position.
- **"Unforeseen" ground conditions.** The report itself says the site investigation missed the hall footprint entirely, so the conditions were arguably *foreseeable* with adequate investigation. It's worth stating whether historic site records (for example, previous buildings on the school site) were checked. If so, Recommendation 6.2 could add a desk study of site history.
- **Recommendation 6.3** should also cover change control: who at the school can request changes, and a requirement to secure budget before instruction.

## Summary of required corrections

| Issue | Location | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Largest cause stated as ground conditions | §3, §7 | Design changes (28 days) are largest; Council-side causes total 49 days |
| LD figure £45,000 | §4 | Correct to £35,000 |
| Causal claim for two-stage tendering | §5, §6.1, §7 | Acknowledge confounding; downgrade to a pilot or further study |
| Overrun breakdown | §4 | Add cost split by cause |
| Temporary accommodation cost | §4 | Report it |

With these corrections, the report would give Members a fair account. In its current form, it understates the Council's own contribution to the delay, overstates the damages to be recovered, and recommends a policy change that its evidence doesn't support.
